I've read that in blind people that read braille the vision part of the brain starts interpreting the tactile signals of their fingertips.

The drawing/painting thing is simple, it's just flattening what we see (or imagine).

In some cases, it involves reducing things to outlines (the edges, sorta like what you perceive by running the side of the cane around an object) plus some additional lines to add details (where the direction of the surfaces change significantly (like in between two walls), or where materials or colors etc change)); some other styles are a bit more complicated, but it's basically the same thing, but adding colors at each spot, or adding more detailed lines to represent shading (areas that are closer to light sources, or surfaces that are aimed more at light sources tend to be lighter, and so are represented with lighter colors or less lines/dots (assuming the drawing is being done with a dark color ink/pencil, and the paper/canvas is light), and the other way around for surfaces that are facing more away, or that have other objects between them and lights).

Oh, and there is an aspect that is a little harder to describe; that's perspective. Things appear smaller when they're further away. To get an idea of why that is, imagine you got a big box, say, the size of a bed; when it is close to you, there are many directions you can throw a ball that will still hit the box; now move the box further from you, and there are a lot less directions that still lead to the box; that's sorta what happens with light, but it's the other way around (light is coming from the "box" into our eyes).

First a note - the distinction between "ethics" and "morality" is something that I have no desire to get into at this moment, or possibly ever. What I am addressing here is the system,whatever it might be, by which individuals determine that a particular action is "right" or "wrong" (or whatever synonyms, rough or otherwise, they might choose to use in place of those terms). For that, I choose to use the word "ethics," since "morality" generally has too much baggage. So know that when I speak of "ethics" I'm speaking of the broad categorization of right and wrong - not narrow, codified standards of behavior.

So... ethics...

As I noted in the thread on the individual, I reject nominal constraints on human behavior that purport to apply to others, primarily (though not entirely) on purely practical grounds. No individual can fully control the behavior of any other individual, so any guide to behavior that presumes such control is meaningless at best. All such guides to behavior, in my estimation, can only meaningfully apply to whatever actions are directly under ones own control.

Or, more simply, ethics isn't about what someone else should do or not do - it's about what the individual who holds the view should do or not do. My ethical views cannot - literally cannot - control your behavior. They can only, and only if I choose to do so, control my own behavior.

A quick aside I've written about elsewhere - this is the elephant in the room in most discussions of ethics (and morality). Most of them fail because the people who are involved are really not seeking the best or most practical method to judge their own actions, but the seemingly best justification for enforcing their judgments of the actions of others.

I'm not going to do that here.

The problem with most ethical systems is that they have to be to at least some degree situational, but, as many (often angrily) point out, situational ethics are problematic. For a concrete example - if one states that killing another human is always, with no exceptions, wrong, then one is stating that killing another human when it's the only possible way to save the life of an innocent is always, with no exceptions, wrong. That flies in the face of reason. However, if one does not assert that killing another human is always, with no exceptions, wrong, then one is effectively stating that killing another human is only sometimes wrong, which, as humanity has shown over and over and over again, simply makes it possible for psychopaths to bring about wholesale slaughter simply by gaining enough power to self-servingly define that "sometimes."

So an ethical system, to be workable, has to be able to deal with the fact that it must be applied to a range of different situations, but it has to be that flexible without giving up its absolute quality - without turning it into some murky and formless sludge that can be, and more to the point will be, rearranged to serve the interests of whoever has great enough power and little enough conscience to do so.

I struggled with this for years before I hit on the answer. We already have a system of thought that combines those qualities - absolute and unchanging identity and situational flexibility. What is that system? Mathematics.

Understand first that what follows is not an actual prescription for a specific ethical system - instead, it's the way that I believe ethics should be viewed in order to make them possess the two qualities they must possess - rigidity and flexibility. It's ultimately sort of metaphorical.

The basis of mathematics is numbers, and numbers are absolute and unvarying identifications. No matter what you do with it - what processes you insert it into - 1 remains 1. In fact, mathematics can only work because of that unvarying quality of numbers. The quantity 3 is and will always be the quantity 3, no matter what it's made a part of.

That's the key to a solid yet flexible ethical system. Each course of action one might take - taking the life of another because it's the only way to save the life of an innocent, for instance - is actually composed of a number of discrete acts. In that simple case - taking the life of another AND saving the life of an innocent. And further, those two discrete acts are modified by the fact that the former is stipulated to be the only way to accomplish the latter. All that's necessary to make ethics both solid and flexible is to consider it in the same way that we consider mathematics - what we're actually doing is combining a number of different acts - "integers" so to speak - into one full course of action - an "equation" so to speak. Viewing it that way makes it possible to treat the "integers" as they need to be treated in order to be meaningful - as absolute and unvarying quantitities - while still allowing for the flexibility necessary to arrive at different judgments of the "right" or "wrong" of a particular course of action that involves some combination of those "integers."

This immediately resolves the problem of maintaining both solidity and flexibility. One can still meaningfully state that taking the life of another is always wrong because that's not the entire course of action that's being proposed - that's just one element of it, just as a particular number is just one element of an equation. It's not necessary to even mess about with that murky and self-destructive notion that taking the life of another has to be "sometimes" right and "sometimes" wrong - that determination is what comes from "solving" the entire "equation." So, for instance, the (wrong) act of taking the life of another is set against the (right) act of saving the life of an innocent, and the two are modified by the fact that the former is the only way to ensure the latter, and one arrives at a "solution" to the "equation" that is likely positive, which is to say "right." Or one considers the act of taking the life of another in order to get his wallet, in which case we have the (exactly the same quantity of wrong) act of taking the life of another, except that it's now set against the (wrong) act of taking his wallet, and the "solution" of that "equation" is most certainly negative, which is to say "wrong."

That's exactly the way that we can have ethical standards that are absolute and unwavering (taking the life of another is wrong), yet still make allowance for the unavoidable times at which that "wrong" act is justifiable. It's not because the value of the act in and of itself has changed, but because the "solution" of the "equation" of which it's only one element has changed, due to the other elements in the equation.

I generally feel compelled to note - I'm not proposing an actual, literal mathematical ethical system, in which each and all would be taught that, for instance, "taking the life of another" = -6 and "saving the life of an innocent" = +7. It's just a convenient and, in my estimation, beneficial way of considering ethics, such that they can be, as they need to be, absolute and flexible at the same time.

And this is... I guess about the fourth or fifth time I've tried to explain this in an essay, and it's not the best of the lot. But it'll have to do...
